gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1053t:
Hurricane Katrina, GAO-05-1053T of September 28, 2005, lays out how watchdogs would track the vast relief and rebuild work to come. The storm hit over half a million people in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. It hurt 21 refineries. It cut more than 3 million phone lines and over a thousand cell sites. Flood water bred health and poison risks.

GAO pulls past work on the plans Katrina would test. It then shows how GAO, inspectors general, and state and local auditors split the watch. The aim is one clear map of who checks cash, speed, and fraud as aid flows south.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-353t:
Wildland Fire Management, GAO-05-353T of February 17, 2005, draws on a report of February 14, 2005, on the rising burn of U.S. wild lands. Burned acres have surged in two decades. A past vow to snuff each fire fast let brush pile thick. That brush now feeds vast, fierce blazes. Homes at the wild edge stand in their path.

GAO tells what gains the federal fire arms have made. It tells the tests they face in the next 5 years. Two arms, the Forest Service and Interior, must name their steps and dates to weigh long-term paths and their costs. That ask gives the piece its title.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-443t:
Army plans to rebuild its units into modular brigades are covered in testimony GAO-05-443T, dated March 16, 2005. Modularity would create brigade combat teams with a common design and a larger pool of ready units. The Army put the cost at $48 billion. Of that, $5 billion sat in the fiscal year 2005 supplemental request. GAO reported on the plan, its staffing and gear problems, and its funding path.

By the end of fiscal year 2006 the Army planned to grow from 33 brigades to 43 modular brigade combat teams. New brigades had been set up or were forming in four active divisions. Yet key gear was short, including unmanned aerial vehicles, communications gear, and trucks. Skilled staff, such as intelligence analysts, would take years to train. Some choices that could raise needs were still open. The testimony shows a fast plan with open questions on cost and readiness.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-453t:
The case for postal reform law is made in testimony GAO-05-453T, presented on April 14, 2005. GAO had placed the Postal Service's long-term outlook on its High-Risk List in April 2001. A presidential commission had reached a like view: universal mail service was at risk without broad change. GAO reported on progress since 2001 and on the areas a reform law should cover.

The Service had made real progress on some of its hardest problems. Even so, GAO said a new law was still needed. Reform should clarify the Service's mission, strengthen oversight and openness, and improve how rates are set. It should also help the Service reshape its network and workforce in a rational way. Without such steps, GAO warned of a taxpayer bailout or sharp rate rises. The testimony lays out the reform agenda item by item.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-473t:
Financial management weaknesses at Head Start programs are the focus of GAO testimony GAO-05-473T, given on April 5, 2005. In fiscal year 2004 the program served 919,000 poor children through 1,680 grantees, backed by $6.8 billion. News of misuse at some local programs put federal oversight in question. The testimony covers risk assessment, data reliability, and whether problems get corrected on time.

Different parts of the Administration for Children and Families each gather data on grantees. Nothing brings those streams together into one risk picture. Site reviews do not always match agency guidance. Figures that grantees report each year go unchecked. More than half the grantees faulted on money rules failed such rules again at the next review. Weak performance and funding were also poorly linked. Grantees that ran programs badly were rarely removed. The testimony makes the case for one full risk system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-483t:
Progress under the federal computer security law is reviewed in testimony GAO-05-483T, presented on April 7, 2005. Poor security in federal systems has sat on GAO's high-risk list since 1997. Congress answered with the Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002. The act set duties for agencies, reviews, and reports to Congress. GAO summed up what the budget office, agencies, and inspectors general reported for fiscal year 2004.

More systems met security duties in 2004 than in 2003, the data showed. Agencies had certified and approved more systems for use. Staff training had also grown in some areas. Still, approval quality varied a great deal. Steps to fix flaws worked well at some agencies and poorly at others. Ten agencies reported fewer staff getting advanced security training. GAO said the yearly reports could be made more useful. It raised a common frame for inspector general reviews.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-493t:
Federal testing of postal sites for anthrax after the 2001 mail attacks is assessed in testimony GAO-05-493T, given on April 5, 2005. Letters carrying anthrax spores had reached two senators and news outlets. 22 people caught the disease and 5 died. The Postal Service, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Environmental Protection Agency sampled 286 postal sites. GAO judged their methods and the trust the results deserve.

Teams sampled spots where spores seemed most likely to settle, like mail handling areas. They did not use random sampling, which can support a firm clean claim for a site. Tests at the 286 sites came back almost all negative. A negative result does not prove a site is free of spores. The sampling and lab steps had never been formally validated. Low levels of anthrax can still sicken or kill some people. GAO said the agencies needed proven methods before negative results could carry weight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-533t:
What the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act catches, and what it misses, is revisited in testimony GAO-05-533T, presented on April 14, 2005. The 1995 act forces cost reports on federal rules that push spending onto states, local bodies, and firms. It does not block such rules. GAO drew on two earlier studies. One tested how the act was applied to laws and rules of 2001 and 2002. The other gathered views from 52 informed parties.

Few items cross the act's cost thresholds. In those two years, only 5 of 377 statutes and 9 of 122 major rules were flagged as holding mandates. Yet at least 43 other statutes and 65 other rules imposed new costs that many would call mandates. Definitions, exceptions, and side routes around review explain much of the gap. Coverage was the point parties raised most. Many said its many carve-outs leave out acts with real impact. Views on other fixes split by sector.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-573t:
Management troubles inside the Department of Homeland Security are catalogued in testimony GAO-05-573T, presented on April 20, 2005. The department joins the nation's security work with federal, state, local, and private partners. GAO placed its transformation on the high-risk list in 2003. This testimony explains why the label was given and lists the management problems that keep the department under close watch.

Three facts drove the high-risk call. The department had to fuse 22 agencies into one while building partnerships and management muscle. It inherited hard operational and management problems from those agencies. Failure would carry grave costs for national security. Some progress has been made since 2003, GAO said. The label stays. The challenge list runs from focus and planning to people, money, and technology. Buying well and steering research are also on it. The testimony argues that missions cannot outrun the management base beneath them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-623t:
A subsidy to help homes buy digital TV gear is scouted in GAO testimony GAO-05-623T (May 26, 2005). When analog broadcasts end, sets without converters go dark. GAO takes no stance on whether to pay. It maps the hard parts: deciding who qualifies, and making sure they hear about the help and what gear counts. Proof of income or of reliance on rooftop antennas would be hard to check.

Choices run from tax credits to vouchers, rebates, or handing out boxes. GAO studied three rebate and three voucher schemes. Vouchers aimed at low-income homes; rebates did not test income.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-643t:
Prepackaged news stories from federal agencies are ruled covert propaganda in this testimony, GAO-05-643T of May 12, 2005. Agencies send stations ready-made segments with hired actors posing as reporters and scripts for anchors to read. Viewers cannot tell the pieces are government-made. The law bars spending public funds on publicity or propaganda Congress has not approved. GAO reads that bar to forbid hiding the government's hand.

Two rulings in the past year found breaches by the health department and the drug control office. Neither segment named its maker. The testimony explains the test GAO applies and why disclosure to viewers is the line.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-653t:
Products sold to beat urine drug tests are the subject of GAO testimony GAO-05-653T, dated May 17, 2005. Four kinds crowd the market: drinks and additives that dilute a sample, cleansers taken in advance, chemicals that destroy drug traces, and substitute urine, real or synthetic. Sellers pitch them openly online to workers facing screens like the federal workplace program.

The testimony sums up what GAO shoppers found about how easy the goods are to buy and how they are marketed. It lays out the tricks each kind uses, so lawmakers can judge whether sales should be curbed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-683t:
GAO-05-683T of June 16, 2005 carries the contractor tax findings of GAO-05-637 into testimony form. About 33,000 firms hired by civilian agencies owed over $3 billion in unpaid federal taxes as of September 30, 2004. GAO investigated 50 firms and found abusive or possibly criminal conduct at all of them. Payroll taxes withheld from wages were kept, a felony, and in one case sent to a foreign bank to build a house.

One owner ran about 20 firms with unpaid taxes on over 300 returns. The testimony names the levy scheme's legal and policy gaps that let debts ride while federal payments flow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-723t:
On June 8, 2006, GAO presented GAO-05-723T on the Defense Department's long-running money and business problems. Eight defense program areas sat on GAO's high-risk list. The department also shared six more government-wide high-risk areas. Congress asked for the scale of the flaws, the cost of business systems, and laws that could help reform.

GAO said weak controls waste billions of dollars each year. They also block clear, auditable money records and hurt mission work. One case hit wounded reserve troops, who lost pay and care when they were wrongly taken off active duty. GAO held that reform needs steady top leadership over many years. Without it, past fixes keep failing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-743t:
GAO-05-743T is a statement presented on May 26, 2005, on the care hospitals give for free. Tax law once required charity care for tax-exempt status. That strict rule ended, and other community gains now count. Congress asked if nonprofit hospitals give more free care than other kinds. GAO used 2003 data from five states.

GAO compared government, nonprofit, and for-profit hospitals. Free care means charity care plus bad debt. GAO found free care costs bunched in a small share of hospitals. In Texas, the top quarter of hospitals bore about 50 percent of such costs. Hospitals of all kinds reported a wide range of other community gains. How they reported those gains varied a lot.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-853t:
Passport fraud detection is faulted in testimony GAO-05-853T, given June 29, 2005. State issued about 8.8 million passports in 2004. That year, its security bureau arrested about 500 people for passport fraud. About 300 were convicted. Fraud often paves the way for other crimes, from drug runs to alien smuggling. GAO studied how fraud is done and what blocks detection.

GAO found stolen identities are the main method used. False claims of lost or damaged passports are another. Terror watch list data is not shared with State in a routine way. Names of wanted persons are also not routinely passed on. GAO tested 67 fugitives and found 37 missing from State's lookout database. One was on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list. Staff cuts and no central fraud library add to the strain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-863t:
Flu pandemic challenges return in testimony GAO-05-863T, presented June 30, 2005. Vaccine shortages hit the 2004-05 season and prior ones. Bird flu activity in Asia raised wider fears. A federal estimate holds that a mid-level pandemic could kill up to 207,000 people in the United States. It could affect 15 to 35 percent of the population. Costs could run from $71 billion to $167 billion.

The testimony rests on GAO work since 2000, plus live work on vaccine supply. GAO laid out the challenges in preparing for and answering a pandemic. It drew lessons from past flu seasons for the bigger event. The focus stays on readiness: vaccine supply, planning, and emergency response. Readers get the state of play as officials braced for a threat whose scale cannot be predicted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-903t:
Health tracking during deployments is the topic of testimony GAO-05-903T, delivered July 19, 2005. After the 1991 Gulf War, studies of unexplained illness stalled for lack of data. Exposure records were thin or missing. In 1997, the Defense Department built a military-wide health surveillance framework. One part tracks workplace and environmental hazards in the field. The testimony rests on a GAO report on that system.

GAO presented findings on how the services carried out the tracking rules in Iraq. It covered what hazard data was gathered and reported during the deployment. It also covered work to use those reports now and later. Such reports serve two ends: quick fixes for units in the field, and a record for long-term health questions. The title states the verdict: the surveillance needs improvement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-923t:
Wildland fire management gets a five-year review in testimony GAO-05-923T, delivered July 14, 2005. Fires grow fiercer as excess brush and trees build up. Federal fire spending tripled from about $1 billion in fiscal year 1999 to nearly $3 billion in fiscal year 2005. Experts warn the window to act is closing fast. The testimony draws mainly on a January 2005 GAO report.

GAO found real progress in data, modeling, and fire behavior research. New tools can now support sharper estimates of fuel-cutting options and their costs. A cost-focused analysis system is ready to back local fire plans. GAO urged open, joint framing of the options. Shared assumptions give the best shot at agreed, accurate figures. Naming long-term options and funding needs in time is critical, GAO held. A Western governors' report reached like findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1113t:
Business tax reform is argued for in GAO-06-1113T, testimony presented on September 20, 2006. Business income taxes supply a large share of federal revenue. Firms also collect much tax from individuals through withholding and reporting. It skews investment choices and weighs down the economy. Its complexity raises planning and record costs, aids shelters, and shields cheats. The statement rests on past GAO work and a review of other studies.

GAO placed the debate against the nation's long-term fiscal imbalance. Without policy change, the gap between spending and revenue will widen. Against that backdrop, the testimony sets out what is wrong with business taxation today. It then offers principles to guide reform. Simpler rules and more uniform treatment across business types would pay off, GAO argued. The statement gives lawmakers a shared frame for a debate that mixes revenue, fairness, and growth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1133t:
Early users of health savings accounts share their experience in GAO-06-1133T, testimony from September 2006. These accounts pair with high-deductible health plans. The plans form a small but growing slice of the private market. Their new design raised questions about how buyers shop for care and what they pay. The statement rests on GAO's August 2006 report on consumer-directed health plans.

GAO compared the cost features of these plans with standard preferred provider plans. It compared who signs up, and how their traits differ from other enrollees. It tracked how much money went into the accounts and how the funds were used. It also reported what enrollees said about their plans, both good and bad. The testimony gives an early, ground-level view of a market experiment. It helps lawmakers weigh savings claims against the risk that patients skip care they need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-113t:
The Defense Department's supply chain, long flagged as high risk, is the subject of GAO-06-113T, testimony from October 2005. GAO put DOD supply management on its high-risk list in 1990. Weak forecasts, poor distribution, and low asset visibility have hurt support for troops. DOD and the budget office built a joint plan to fix those three areas. GAO gave its views on the plan and on what lasting repair requires.

Supply failures carry real costs. DOD moved over 2 million tons of cargo for the Iraq war, yet shortages of items like tires hampered operations. Its supply inventory grew from $62.3 billion in fiscal year 2001 to $77.4 billion in fiscal year 2004. GAO called the DOD plan a good start and a sound framework. Success, though, needs steady top leadership, firm resource pledges, and clear performance measures. GAO promised to track progress in its high-risk reviews.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-183t:
Flood insurance oversight is reprised in GAO-06-183T, testimony presented on October 20, 2005. The statement draws on a report issued earlier that week, plus past GAO work. The National Flood Insurance Program, run by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, dates to 1968. Hurricanes Katrina, Rita, Ivan, and Isabel had just battered the Gulf and East coasts. GAO covered coverage limits, the agency's monitoring of insurers, and its slow work on the 2004 reform law.

Coverage caps leave many owners short after a flood. A home worth more than $250,000 cannot be insured to full value. The agency reviews 95 private insurers that sell its policies. Its file sampling lacked a valid method, so review results could not be projected. Key 2004 reforms missed their December 30, 2004 deadline. The agency had no plan with milestones to finish them. GAO also repeated that the program is not actuarially sound by design.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-233t:
Security clearance reform gets a progress check in GAO-06-233T, testimony presented on November 9, 2005. The Defense Department handles about 2 million clearances for staff, troops, and contractors. A leaked secret can do grave harm, so the stakes are high. Long delays and weak quality put the program on GAO's high-risk list in January 2005. In February the department handed its investigations to the personnel office. Waits for a top secret clearance then ran over a year. A June order gave the budget office the lead on a fix plan.

GAO gave an early review of that plan. It tested the plan against sound planning standards. It asked how far the plan cures slow, uneven clearance work. Some old problems are addressed, GAO said, but concerns remain. The testimony lists what must happen before the program leaves the high-risk list. Speed means little if checks turn sloppy, so both matter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-253t:
How Social Security numbers go to the foreign-born is explained in GAO-06-253T, testimony presented on March 2, 2006. About 35.7 million foreign-born people lived in the United States in 2004. Many hold numbers by right, and a number can prove the right to work. Some numbers, though, have been given wrongly. New laws aim to guard the number and curb fraud. A House panel asked GAO two plain questions: who qualifies for a number, and who qualifies for benefits.

The agency checks immigration papers before it issues a number, GAO said. It also marks some cards as valid for work only with federal permission. A third kind is not valid for work at all. By 2003 the agency had issued slightly more than 7 million of those non-work cards. People use them to claim benefits they are due. GAO made no new recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-283t:
Deep flaws in veterans' disability claims are laid out in GAO-06-283T, testimony presented on December 7, 2005. The House veterans panel asked GAO to report on the claims system's troubles and its chances to improve. Waits run long, backlogs grow, and errors mar decisions. Average payments swing widely from state to state, which hints at uneven rulings. In January 2003 GAO put federal disability programs on its high-risk list. The process for judging claims is one cause.

The rating method rests on an old view of how injuries limit work, GAO said. Medicine and technology now let many people with disabilities live and work with more freedom. The system has not kept pace with that change. Modernizing it is part of the fix, along with faster and steadier decisions. The testimony gathers years of GAO findings into one charge sheet. It frames reform as a debt owed to those who served.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-333t:
Nursing home care for aging veterans, and the strain ahead, fill GAO-06-333T, testimony given January 9, 2006. The veterans department runs or funds care in three settings. Community homes and state veterans' homes serve the rest under its pay. In 2004, 38 percent of veterans were over 65, against 12 percent of the public. A 1999 law obliges the department to provide this care to set groups. GAO updated its earlier findings with fiscal 2005 figures.

The statement tracks spending and patient counts across the settings. State and community homes carry almost two-thirds of the workload. Yet data on who qualifies and how long they stay lag there. GAO urged the department to close that gap in 2004; the work is unfinished. Planning blind is the core risk. Demand will swell as the veteran population ages further. The testimony asks whether the system can see its own future.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-403t:
Fast disaster aid can save families, and fast aid can also invite fraud. The testimony numbered GAO-06-403T, delivered February 13, 2006, reports on expedited help after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita. The Federal Emergency Management Agency paid $2,000 per household under its Individuals and Households Program. Total program payments reached about $5.4 billion by mid-December 2005. Expedited aid made up $2.3 billion of that sum.

GAO tested controls meant to limit aid to qualified applicants. It looked for signs of fraud and abuse in claims and payments. It also checked controls over debit cards. GAO found control weaknesses exposed the government to much fraud. Readers get amounts and failure points.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-453t:
Hundreds of billions in tax owed never reach the Treasury on time. The testimony numbered GAO-06-453T, delivered February 15, 2006, explains the tax gap. The Internal Revenue Service put the gross gap at $345 billion. It expects to recover part of that sum later. The net gap is estimated at $290 billion. The gap comes from underreporting, underpaying, and not filing returns.

Senate budget leaders asked GAO to explain causes and possible fixes. GAO addresses the nature and scale of the gap. It sets out steps that may help close it. Big progress rests on stronger current techniques and new laws, GAO said. Readers also get long-term fiscal context.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-513t:
Phone and internet access on tribal lands lags, and the reasons are tangled. On March 7, 2006, testimony GAO-06-513T drew on a January 2006 GAO report. A goal of the Communications Act of 1934 is access to telecommunications for all Americans. The testimony reviews service levels for Native Americans living on tribal lands. It also lists federal programs meant to improve service there.

GAO describes barriers that block improvement. It shows how some tribes are tackling those barriers themselves. The statement frames the core problem in its title. Assessing and improving service on tribal lands faces real challenges. Readers get status, programs, and local responses in one account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-523t:
A second March statement returns to two fighter programs and their weak business cases. Testimony GAO-06-523T, dated March 28, 2006, updates Congress on the F-22A and Joint Strike Fighter. Together the programs carry an estimated cost of almost $320 billion. They aim to replace tactical fighters, many over 20 years old. Overruns have cut buying power and delayed capability for troops.

GAO judges how far the current business cases can be executed. It reports the status of the wider tactical aircraft renewal effort. It sets out options as the department moves forward. The renewal goals are not supported by knowledge-based business cases, GAO said. Readers can compare this update with the earlier March testimony.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-553t:
A new department building its finance systems can learn from other agencies' failures. In testimony GAO-06-553T (March 29, 2006), GAO covers financial management systems at the Department of Homeland Security. GAO was asked to give its views for a hearing. A recent GAO report cataloged big problems in past agency system efforts. This statement discusses those recurring problems. It points out key modernization challenges at the department.

GAO also highlights building blocks for success. Those blocks form the base for sound system work. The department has a chance to use best practices, GAO said. Readers get failure patterns and success factors in one statement. The focus is prevention, not blame.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-563t:
In a small test, GAO staff took tax returns to chain preparers and found big mistakes. In testimony GAO-06-563T (April 4, 2006), GAO reports that limited study. Little data exist on the quality of paid preparers' work. Preparers range from enrolled agents approved by the tax agency to unenrolled chain staff. GAO had returns prepared at 19 outlets of several chains. It also analyzed agency data and reviewed how preparers are regulated.

GAO describes what marks returns done by paid preparers. It explains what government regulation exists for them. It shows issues taxpayers may meet when using them. Serious errors were made, GAO found. The study is limited, and GAO says so.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-573t:
Weather satellites in polar orbit watch storms, oceans, and climate. Delivered March 30, 2006, testimony GAO-06-573T reports on the planned successor system. The National Polar-orbiting Operational Environmental Satellite System would merge two current systems into one. It is meant to keep data flowing for forecasting and climate work through 2020. Three agencies run a joint program office for it. They are the weather agency, the Defense Department, and the space agency.

Cost increases have triggered a review of the program. Its direction is on hold, the title says. GAO was asked to give the program's current status and plans. It also discusses points to weigh in moving forward. Readers get a status snapshot.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-583t:
This statement reports the border test in spoken form, at two locations. The testimony numbered GAO-06-583T, delivered March 28, 2006, covers investigators who transported radioactive sources across U.S. borders. Customs and Border Protection uses detection gear at ports of entry to stop such entry. Most travelers enter through the nation's 154 land border ports. Inspectors there check travelers and hunt contraband, including weapons of mass destruction. Congress requested the investigation amid high public interest in border security.

The premise is stated plainly in the text. Borders must be protected from smuggling of radioactive sources by terrorists. Readers can compare this statement with the companion letter report. It gives the inspector mission and test setting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-653t:
Modernizing the nation's air traffic control system is covered in GAO-06-653T, testimony GAO gave on June 21, 2006. The Federal Aviation Administration's modernization effort has sat on GAO's high risk list for more than a decade. Two newer bodies inside the agency share the work. The Air Traffic Organization runs the current system, and a joint planning office designs the next generation system.

GAO said the Air Traffic Organization had made promising moves toward running like a performance-based business. Its buying and management processes were improving. But the body was barely two years old, and GAO warned that the new habits were not yet firmly in place. GAO also noted that planning for the next generation system was still at an early stage.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-703t:
How AIDS funding is shared across the nation is questioned in GAO-06-703T, testimony dated April 27, 2006. The Ryan White CARE Act sends funds to states and cities for care and drugs. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that between 1,039,000 and 1,185,000 people lived with HIV or AIDS at the end of 2003. That count included 415,193 people with AIDS as of December 2004. Funding formulas, though, rested in part on older case data.

GAO said changes were needed to improve the distribution of funding. Places where the epidemic had grown did not always get a matching share. GAO's findings fed the debate over renewing the act. The testimony shows how stale data can skew aid away from current need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-773t:
Foreign doctors in shortage areas are covered in GAO-06-773T, testimony presented on May 18, 2006. Many United States communities struggle to attract physicians. Foreign doctors who train in the United States on J-1 visas must normally go home for two years. Waivers let some stay and practice in underserved areas instead. GAO shared preliminary findings on how widely these waivers are used.

GAO found that waivers remain a major means of placing doctors in underserved areas. More than 1,000 waivers were requested in each of the past three years. The requests covered nearly every state. In fiscal year 2005, states made more than 90 percent of the requests. About 44 percent of state requests sent doctors to practice only in underserved areas. The findings frame a key pipeline for rural care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-803t:
The Capitol Visitor Center returns in GAO-06-803T, testimony presented on May 24, 2006. The underground center was meant to welcome visitors and screen them away from the Capitol itself. GAO tracked the project's milestones and schedule since the hearing of April 27, 2006. It also reviewed steps the Architect of the Capitol had taken on risks. This statement is one of a series of monthly updates GAO gave Congress on the project.

GAO reported that construction kept moving forward in the month since April. The project team still proposed the same opening dates. The base center would open in April 2007, with House and Senate expansion spaces in May 2007. GAO repeated its view from March and April. The dates, GAO said, leave too little time for critical finishing work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-833t:
Data breaches and how agencies should react fill GAO-06-833T, testimony GAO presented on June 8, 2006. A breach at the Department of Veterans Affairs had just exposed personal data on millions of veterans. The case showed how fast private facts can escape federal files. GAO set out steps agencies can take to prevent improper disclosures. GAO also addressed how to respond when prevention fails.

GAO said agencies can lower the odds that personal databases are compromised. One key step is the privacy impact assessment, a study of how a system collects, stores, and shares personal data. Such reviews are needed whenever technology handles such information. Limiting what is collected and guarding it well are companion duties. The testimony gives agencies a practical checklist for a rising risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-843t:
Diversity trends in finance are restated in GAO-06-843T, testimony presented on July 12, 2006. The statement draws on GAO's report on the financial services industry from 1993 through 2004. It tracks who holds management jobs in banks, insurers, and related firms. It also reviews the steps firms took to widen those ranks. The data come from employer reports filed with the equal employment agency.

GAO found that overall management diversity did not change substantially over the period. Some minority groups, though, gained more ground than others. Employer data show minority representation in management rose from 11.1 percent to 15.5 percent. Gains for minority women and men drove much of that shift. African-American representation also rose. The testimony gives Congress the headline figures from the longer report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-863t:
Internet recovery planning is restated for a new panel in GAO-06-863T, testimony GAO delivered on July 28, 2006. The Internet grew from a government research project into the backbone of national business. Private firms now own and run the vast majority of its infrastructure. Federal policy calls for a joint plan to restore service after a crippling disruption. The Homeland Security Department holds that task. GAO summarized the challenges it faces.

GAO explained that a major outage could come from a physical blow, a cyber incident, or both. Recent events had caused local and regional disruptions, which showed the need for recovery plans. Writing one plan across government and private owners is the hard part. Roles, priorities, and trust must be settled before a crisis. The testimony repeats GAO's core findings from its June report on the subject.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-933t:
Sharing of security news among port partners is the focus of GAO testimony GAO-06-933T, dated July 10, 2006. Ports are rich targets, and many levels of government share guard duty there. News that moves late or half-formed can leave gaps.

GAO found that sharing efforts were improving. Port security committees had gained in speed and fullness of what they pass on. Joint operations centers also helped crews pool and spread facts. Yet form varied by port, and lack of security clearances could bar some partners. The testimony shows a guard network learning to talk, with clear strain points left.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-953t:
Rebuilding Iraq needs a fuller national plan, GAO argues in testimony GAO-06-953T, dated July 11, 2006. The National Strategy for Victory in Iraq was the U.S. guide for that effort. GAO set the plan, and its backing papers, against what a sound plan should hold.

The plan named its purpose, scope, risks, and threats well enough. It spoke of goals and acts, though with less depth. It part-met tests on who owns each task, on work with the Iraqi government, and on future costs. GAO warned that a plan spread across many papers is hard to use. Other GAO work on security and politics fills out the picture.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-983t:
Military supply chain flaws, a GAO high-risk item since 1990, are revisited in testimony GAO-06-983T, dated July 25, 2006. The supply chain can decide wins and losses at the front line. Its cost is vast. In 2005 the Defense Department set a fix plan with three planks: forecast needs, track gear, and move supplies.

In October 2005 GAO called the plan a good first step. Now it gave views on headway in putting the plan to work. It checked the measures used to show gains. It also set the plan beside other defense logistics plans. Hurdles remain, GAO said, in both making and proving progress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1003t:
Computer security at the Department of Homeland Security is the topic of GAO testimony GAO-07-1003T, dated June 20, 2007. The department was formed in 2002 from 22 agencies. Its border arm guards the nation's edges. Both lean on computer systems for their work and assets.

GAO has called weak computer security a government-wide high risk since 1997. The testimony sets out the department's security program. It checks the guards on key systems at the department and its border arm. It rests on agency, inspector general, and GAO reports, some still in draft. The picture is of a young department with old security flaws to close.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1023t:
Wide use of Social Security numbers, and their weak guard, is the topic of GAO testimony GAO-07-1023T, dated June 21, 2007. The number has grown far past its first aim. Public and private bodies now use it as a go-to ID for many ends.

With a name and birth date, the number is a key tool for identity theft. GAO set out how agencies use the number. It set out how firms use it. It named the flaws that still leave numbers exposed. The testimony rests on GAO work from 2002 to 2006. It frames a plain trade-off: handy ID, shared by all, is hard to keep safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1033t:
Seller-funded help with home down payments is examined in GAO testimony GAO-07-1033T, dated June 22, 2007. The Federal Housing Administration lets buyers take aid from charities whose funds come in part from home sellers. Other big mortgage players bar that path.

GAO told Congress how use of such aid with insured loans has trended. It set out how the aid reshapes the purchase deal, and what it does to house prices. It weighed how loans with such aid perform over time. The findings rest on GAO's November 2005 report, GAO-06-24. Aid of this kind, GAO found, harms loan performance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1043t:
Beach water safety under a 2000 law is the topic of GAO testimony GAO-07-1043T, dated June 27, 2007. Germs in water and sand can sicken beach users. The BEACH Act gives states federal grants to test beach water and warn the public.

The statement sums up GAO's May 2007 report on the Great Lakes. GAO judged how far the Environmental Protection Agency has put the act in place. It heard doubts on the grant split formula. It told how Great Lakes states built their test and warning work with the grants. Headway is real, GAO said, but added steps could guard health better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1063t:
Address lists for the 2010 Census are the topic of GAO testimony GAO-07-1063T, dated June 26, 2007. The Census Bureau asks state, local, and tribal bodies to update maps and lists of homes. That program is called the Local Update of Census Addresses, or LUCA.

GAO told where LUCA stands. It set out the bureau's reply to past GAO points on the program. It flagged fresh hurdles in the work. The testimony rests on a GAO report dated June 14, 2007. It draws on program papers, a poll of dress rehearsal players, and talks with bureau and local staff. Headway is real, but gains are still needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1073t:
Beach safety law gets a second GAO airing in testimony GAO-07-1073T, dated July 12, 2007. Germs in beach water and sand can harm health. The BEACH Act of 2000 funds state programs to test water and warn swimmers. The Environmental Protection Agency runs the grants.

The statement sums up GAO's May 2007 report on the Great Lakes. GAO judged how far the agency has put the act's terms in place. It aired doubts on the grant split formula. It told how Great Lakes states used grant funds to build test and alert work. Headway is clear, GAO said, but more steps could guard health.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1083t:
Mail plant reshaping at the U.S. Postal Service is updated in GAO testimony GAO-07-1083T, dated July 26, 2007. Mail habits shifted, and the service must cut costs and work with more speed. It is reshaping its plant network to match, merging some sites.

GAO had reported headway in that work in a recent review. Hurdles stay, such as keeping service norms and facing town pushback. The testimony sets out what changed in the network. It gives GAO doubts on the reshape plan and on site mergers. It adds doubts on how the service gauges delivery speed. Better joining of parts, and better gauges, are still needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1163t:
Air funding gets a further GAO statement in testimony GAO-07-1163T, dated August 1, 2007. The Federal Aviation Administration runs a safe but strained air system. A joint office plans its next era form, NextGen. Current law for the agency, its trust fund, and most of its taxes ends September 30, 2007.

Bills H.R. 2881 and S. 1300 name varied income paths, from taxes to flight fees. GAO asked how far the current funding shape can bear agency work, NextGen among it. It set out points that could move NextGen's cost. It weighed the effects of picked funding plans. Stable finance, GAO notes, is itself a high-risk need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1243t:
Unemployment insurance is meant to carry workers through a job loss. GAO testified on who actually gets those benefits in GAO-07-1243T, dated September 19, 2007. The statement builds on GAO's September 2007 report on benefit receipt. GAO studied Labor Department data and a national Census Bureau survey. It compared receipt rates across wage levels and work schedules.

GAO found that the share of jobless workers getting benefits rose modestly from the mid-1980s to 2005. Even so, it stayed below the near-50 percent rate of the 1950s. Low-wage workers were far less likely to receive benefits than higher-wage workers. In the early 1990s they were about half as likely to receive them. By 1998 and 2003, they were only about one-third as likely. That gap had not narrowed over time, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1253t:
Planning for responder health care after the World Trade Center attack fell short in lasting ways. That was GAO's message in testimony GAO-07-1253T on September 20, 2007. The statement rests mainly on GAO's July 2007 report on responder health programs. It covers the federal screening program for responders who were federal workers. It also covers care for nonfederal responders outside the New York City area. A third topic was lessons learned for future disasters.

GAO said problems remained in planning for and providing services. The federal screening program had been set up, suspended, and resumed over the years. Workers outside New York still lacked assured access to screening and monitoring. GAO had urged the health secretary to act quickly to close those gaps. The testimony closes by drawing lessons from the World Trade Center programs. Those lessons aim to guide health planning after future disasters.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-233t:
Workers sickened by radiation at nuclear weapons sites have waited years for compensation rulings. GAO summed up its past findings in testimony GAO-07-233T on December 5, 2006. A 2000 law set up the compensation program. The Energy Department ran one part and Labor runs the other. A science agency rebuilds each worker's radiation dose. An advisory board checks that science. A budget office memo had raised fears of cost cutting.

GAO's May 2004 report found a slow start and a claim backlog, the testimony recalls. Many claimants could wait years for a ruling. The board's review contractor posed a second worry. In its first 2 years, it spent almost 90 percent of a $3 million, 5-year budget. Spending was poorly tracked at first. GAO also flagged conflict-of-interest risks around the board. The testimony points to oversight fixes still needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-343t:
Poverty touched 37 million Americans in 2005, about 13 percent of the population. GAO summed up the research on its costs in testimony GAO-07-343T on January 24, 2007. The statement rests on a review of economic literature. It covers studies by academics, think tanks, and agencies. Experts reviewed the draft before release. The testimony asks two questions. It asks how poverty links to health, crime, and work. It also asks how poverty links to growth.

Research ties poverty to worse health and more crime, GAO reports. It also ties poverty to weaker attachment to jobs. Poor areas grow more slowly than rich ones on average. The evidence suggests poverty drags on the wider economy. Program costs form only part of the burden. Lost productivity adds a second, larger channel. The full report behind the statement carries the study details.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-433t: Older workers were an untapped asset in 2007, and GAO's briefing collects the best practices for engaging and keeping them. The testimony shares what worked. The findings argue that experience is a resource, not a retirement date. The gray heads held the know-how.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-453t: Homeland Security's buying shop needed a tune-up in 2007, and GAO's briefing eyes the department's acquisition setup. The testimony probes the purchasing. The findings warn that the security state's shopping cart needed adult supervision. The checkbook had to match the mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-543t: The watchdog passed its own hat in 2007 — GAO's briefing lays out its budget request for the coming year. The testimony justifies the ask line by line. The findings show the auditor practicing the transparency it preaches to every other agency.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-583t: Passenger trains were soft targets in 2007, and GAO's briefing says a federal strategy with better coordination was needed to guide security. The testimony demands the plan in detail. The findings warn that the rails carried millions with too little guarding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-633t: The gas-tanker spill question would not go away in 2007 — GAO's briefing again says the public-safety fallout of an LNG disaster needed spelling out. The testimony repeats the demand. The findings insist the ports deserve the worst-case numbers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-683t: The security department's far-flung teams needed a leader to knit them together in 2007 — GAO's briefing says clear orders from the ops chief would get the units working as one. The testimony pushes for teamwork by design, not by luck. The findings argue that a department is only as strong as its inner ties.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-693t: Rebuilding the skies had a planning office in 2007 — GAO's briefing tracks the joint office's progress and the key issues still ahead. The testimony takes stock of the effort. The findings warn that the future air system needed a much surer hand on the blueprint.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-793t: Tiny towns were losing their lifeline to the sky in 2007 — GAO's briefing lays out the programs and options for keeping air service alive in small communities. The testimony weighs the subsidies. The findings ask what a ticket to the rest of America is worth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-823t: Offshore tax havens were bleeding the Treasury in 2007 — GAO's briefing says ensuring compliance beyond the borders stayed hard for enforcers. The testimony maps the enforcement gaps in full detail. The findings' message stings: the tax haven is the honest taxpayer's insult.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-833t: The giant security department's to-do list was daunting in 2007 — GAO's briefing lays out the top brass's management and program hurdles. The testimony is a frank list of unfinished work. The findings' theme is sobering: sheer size is not the same as being ready.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-873t: Federal health premiums kept climbing in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the growth had finally started to slow. The testimony parses the premium trend for Congress in plain terms. The findings offer a breather, not a victory, in the long health-cost wars.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-933t: Camp Lejeune's water poisoned Marines in 2007's reckoning — GAO's briefing takes up the old contamination at the Corps' storied base. The testimony lays out the health questions. The findings keep faith with the families who drank the water and waited decades for answers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-943t: Navy ship dreams were outrunning business sense in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the fleet's building plans needed realistic price tags first. The testimony demands honest math before the keels are laid. The findings are a shipbuilder's proverb: hope is not a procurement strategy.

gao-gaoreports-gao-08-183t: GAO went back to Congress in 2007 on the weather craft parked over the equator — the sentinels that spot hurricanes brewing. Cost and timing risks still hung over the next batch, GAO said, and the fixes had not landed. The briefing hammers a quiet truth: the storms get watched only if the watchers in orbit stay funded and on track.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-213t: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that the yearly audits of grant spenders kept coming up short. These single audits are the main check on billions in federal grant money — and GAO found the checking itself was sloppy. The briefing calls for a fix to the fixers: better audits, or the grant billions fly with no cop on the beat.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-233t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that bank regulators had barely measured whether their help for minority-owned banks was working. These small banks serve blocks the big lenders skip, and Congress wanted them nursed along. The briefing's sting: good will without yardsticks. Nobody could say if the support was saving banks or just spending money.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-253t: GAO briefed Congress in 2007 on the terror watch lists used at borders, airports, and visa desks. The lists were scattered and the sharing was thin, so GAO urged one tight, well-run net. The briefing captures the post-9/11 drive to turn a pile of rival lists into a single screen no suspect could slip past.
